rationale: LServe's main contribution is a unified block-sparse attention serving system with specialized CUDA/PTX kernels for prefill and decode. It fuses static and dynamic sparse attention patterns and KV-cache quantization into GPU attention kernels, so the optimization is at the attention-kernel level rather than only request scheduling.

The paper adapts ring attention for inference with pass-KV and pass-Q variants, load-balanced input/KV sharding, and runtime selection for long-context prefill and decode. Although distributed-system framed and implemented around existing attention kernels, the primary mechanism changes the attention computation schedule and KV layout across devices.

DynaX proposes dynamic X:M structured pruning and block scheduling for sparse attention computation, which is kernel-like attention acceleration. The abstract frames it as algorithm-hardware co-design around a processing-element array, so without full text it is borderline between a software kernel optimization and a hardware architecture proposal.

Balance is a CPU thread scheduler for DLRM inference that allocates cores to embedding tables, uses MLP-aware task scheduling, and applies work stealing/table reordering. These are runtime/thread orchestration policies rather than new compute kernels, kernel generators, or precision/layout kernels.

Tally is primarily a GPU sharing/performance-isolation system, but its key mechanism is thread-block-level GPU kernel scheduling with slicing and preemption implemented through kernel transformation passes. Because the optimization targets concurrent workload isolation rather than a particular ML operator kernel, it is borderline kernel-style.

COMET integrates MoE communication and expert computation into fused GPU kernels with thread-block specialization and adaptive block assignment. This is explicitly fine-grained communication-computation overlap inside kernels, evaluated for MoE model execution in training/inference settings.

Parendi is an RTL simulator/compiler that partitions and maps hardware simulation onto thousands of IPU cores. Its contributions are simulation partitioning, compilation, and synchronization/communication analysis rather than optimized production compute kernels for an application workload.

The paper focuses on analyzing and optimizing deep-learning operators on Ascend, with case studies and 41 optimized operators integrated into the Ascend operator library. Its roofline model is an analysis tool, but the stated evaluation centers on concrete operator/kernel optimizations across training and inference workloads.

FlashInfer is an attention engine that generates customizable high-performance GPU attention kernels for LLM serving. Its block-sparse KV-cache format, JIT attention template, and dynamic load-balanced scheduler are kernel-level mechanisms for prefill, decode, prefix sharing, and speculative decoding.

SparseTransX reformulates KGE training so the core embedding computation becomes sparse-dense matrix multiplication, replacing scatter/gather-heavy computations with optimized CPU/GPU sparse kernels. The library also applies low-level optimizations such as SIMD vectorization, cache blocking, tiling, and warp-level GPU optimization.

The paper proposes ray virtualization, dynamic treelet queues, and warp repacking as GPU/RT-unit architectural mechanisms for ray tracing, evaluated in simulation. Per the codebook, a hardware/microarchitecture proposal evaluated only in simulation is not a software kernel-style optimization.

BatchZK customizes GPU implementations of ZKP modules such as Merkle tree, sum-check, and linear-time encoder around a fully pipelined execution strategy. The design assigns continuous work to GPU threads, dynamically loads proof data, and overlaps transfers with GPU computation, making it a kernel-level scheduling/layout optimization for proof generation.
